newsitem.title: USA: Supreme Court rules Clinton can be sued.
newsitem.headline: Supreme Court rules Clinton can be sued.

text.p: A unanimous Supreme Court handed President Bill Clinton a stinging defeat on Tuesday, ruling that Paula Jones' sexual harassment lawsuit against him can proceed immediately rather than wait until he leaves office.
In a landmark ruling, all nine justices held for the first time that a lawsuit against a sitting president for conduct unrelated to official duties may proceed to trial.

The nation's highest court rejected Clinton's arguments that allowing the lawsuit to go forward while he remained in the White House would prove a significant distraction, hindering the performance of his presidential duties.
The ruling involved only when the case goes forward, not the merits of Jones' allegations, which Clinton denied.

Jones claimed Clinton made unwanted sexual advances in 1991 in a Little Rock hotel when he was governor of Arkansas and she was a state employee. She claimed Clinton had her summoned during a government conference and when they were alone exposed himself to her and asked her to perform oral sex. Jones sought $700,000 damages.
Clinton's private attorney Robert Bennett, who conceded he was "a little surprised" by the court's unanimous ruling, denied the allegations again on Tuesday, calling them "malicious and false."
"We look forward to our day in court to show these charges are malicious, baseless and politically inspired," he said on the CNN programme "Larry King Live."
Bennett also expressed scepticism an out-of-court settlement would be reached with Jones.
"There's not going to be a settlement if what is required is the president paying money to Paula Jones or acknowledging things that are simply not true," he said.

The ruling sent the case back to a federal judge in Arkansas, where the lawsuit was filed in 1994, for more hearings. But it could be delayed by new motions by Clinton's lawyers seeking to dismiss the lawsuit.
Even so, Gil Davis, one of two attorneys representing Jones, predicted a trial would start "within a year."

U.S. District Judge Susan Webber Wright, who is handling the lawsuit, said she will decide on a trial date within two months, after the Supreme Court remands the case to her court and after Clinton files his response to Jones' complaint.

"In a typical case, the trial setting will be some 10-12 months from the date of the scheduling order, although this time could vary depending on various circumstances," Wright said in a court order issued on Tuesday.

In Paris, where Clinton was signing an accord bewteen NATO leaders and Russian President Boris Yeltsin, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said, "We don't have any comment here, not having analysed the opinion."

Asked if the ruling would detract from the president's agenda, McCurry replied, "I believe that opinion appears to have distracted all of you. But the president continued to conduct the nation's business today."
Jones, in a written statement, welcomed the court's decision. "I am very happy that the U.S. Supreme Court has ruled in my favour and I'm quite pleased that i will have my day in court," she said.

At a news conference with Davis, Joseph Cammarata, Jones' other lawyer, hailed the ruling, saying she was "anxious to have her day in court" to restore her reputation. "The Supreme Court has said today that the president of the United States is just like you and me. We don't have a monarchy, we don't have a king," Cammarata said.

Justice John Paul Stevens said for the court in the 28-page opinion that Clinton's arguments for a delay until he leaves office in 2001 find no support in history, in court precedent or in the U.S. Constitution.

He brushed aside Clinton's concerns that allowing the case to go forward will trigger a wave of other lawsuits, noting that only three incumbent presidents in more than 200 years of U.S. history have faced civil lawsuits for events that occurred before they took office.

The lawsuits against Harry Truman and Theodore Roosevelt were dismissed before they took office in decisions upheld after they became president and a lawsuit against President John Kennedy over an automobile accident was settled.

Stevens rejected arguments that the lawsuit would interfere with presidential duties, saying "We assume that the testimony of the president ... may be taken at the White House at a time that will accommodate his busy schedule, and that, if a trial is held, there would be no necessity for the president to attend in person, though he could elect to do so."
Stevens said delaying the trial until Clinton leaves office could harm Jones, with the potential loss of evidence and the fading of memories of witnesses.
